advice: CDC recommends Tdap in every pregnancy, between weeks 27 and 36 (earlier in that window is preferred). The mother's antibodies pass to the baby and protect it until its own vaccines start at 2 months; Tdap in this window lowers whooping cough risk in babies under 2 months by 78%.
Babies under 1 year are at greatest risk of whooping cough and its severe complications. DTaP is a routine childhood vaccine: doses at 2, 4 and 6 months, with boosters at 15-18 months and 4-6 years.
source_title: CDC: Whooping cough vaccines; CDC child and adolescent schedule notes
status_note: Dose ages are from the 2025 schedule notes page; DTaP remained routine in the 5 Jan 2026 schedule revision.

advice: Everyone around a new baby (parents, siblings, grandparents, babysitters) should be up to date on whooping cough vaccines; teens and adults who have never had Tdap should get one. Get it at least 2 weeks before meeting the baby, as antibodies take about 2 weeks to develop. Siblings and parents are the most common source of whooping cough in young babies.
source_title: CDC: Vaccines for family and caregivers
status_note: Older page (last reviewed 2021); content consistent with current Tdap guidance.

advice: Anyone who cares for a new baby should get a flu vaccine each flu season, at least 2 weeks before meeting the baby. A flu shot during pregnancy also helps protect the baby in its first months.
source_title: CDC: Vaccines for family and caregivers

advice: One way to protect a baby from RSV is the maternal RSV vaccine (Abrysvo) at 32-36 weeks of pregnancy, given September to January in most of the US. Antibodies take about 2 weeks to reach the baby and protect it for about 6 months. It is not currently repeated in a later pregnancy.
source_title: CDC: Immunizations to protect infants from RSV

advice: The other option is an RSV antibody for the baby (nirsevimab or clesrovimab), for babies under 8 months whose mother did not get the RSV vaccine. Babies born October to March get it within a week of birth; others shortly before RSV season. Most babies need one option, not both.
source_title: CDC: Immunizations to protect infants from RSV
status_note: CHECK: the 5 Jan 2026 childhood schedule revision moved infant RSV immunization out of the routine list (high-risk groups / shared decision with a clinician). This CDC page predates that change. Briefing should say: talk to the baby's healthcare provider.

advice: CDC recommends one RSV vaccine dose for everyone 75 and older, and for adults 50-74 at increased risk (e.g. chronic heart or lung disease, weakened immune system, living in a nursing home). It is a single dose, not yearly; late summer to early fall (August-October) is the best time.

People 65 and older face higher risk of serious flu complications (about 70-85% of flu deaths in recent seasons). CDC prefers high-dose, recombinant or adjuvanted flu vaccines for this age group, ideally by the end of October. Anyone 65+ who develops flu symptoms should contact a healthcare provider promptly, as antiviral treatment is recommended for higher-risk people.
source_title: CDC: Flu and people 65 years and older

advice: CDC recommends the 2025-2026 COVID-19 vaccine for people 6 months and older through individual-based decision-making, and says vaccination is especially important for people 65 and older, nursing-home residents and people at high risk of severe COVID-19.
source_title: CDC: Staying up to date with COVID-19 vaccines
status_note: CHECK: refers to the 2025-2026 vaccine; look for a 2026-2027 update before the demo.

advice: CDC says COVID-19 vaccination is especially important during pregnancy and breastfeeding; for children 6 months to 17 years, parents should discuss vaccination with a healthcare provider.
source_title: CDC: Staying up to date with COVID-19 vaccines

advice: If you have respiratory symptoms (fever, cough, runny nose), stay home and away from others. Resume normal activities only after at least 24 hours of improving symptoms with no fever (without fever-reducing medicine), then take extra care for 5 days: cleaner air, hand hygiene, a well-fitted mask, distance and testing, especially around people at higher risk.
source_title: CDC: Preventing spread of respiratory viruses when you're sick

advice: CDC's core prevention steps are staying up to date on vaccines, washing hands, and cleaner air where people gather. Masks, distance and testing add protection when illness is rising in the community or when you are with someone at higher risk.
